messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] repositories in flux
parts:
Daniel and I have been Gchatting about the transition. I don't know git well enough to make sure we're not stepping into quicksand, so I want to throw this out there to see if anyone can spot a problem:

1) Rename master as develop with

git branch -m master develop

2) Create a new master branch starting at the v1.3.0 tag with

git branch master v1.3.0

3) Pushing everything to github with

git push -f origin master

This idea was based largely based on the commentary in these two posts

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2862590/how-to-replace-master-branch-in-git-entirely-from-another-branch
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2763006/change-the-current-branch-to-master-in-git

The central problem with a transition to the gitflow paradigm is that there are an untold number of branches out there in the world that have branched off our master branch prior to today that in the future need to be capable of being merged into develop and subsequently master. I'm theorizing that with the rename in step 1), git would be able to sort that out because the reflog goes with it.

Another issue is that maybe in the next week or two, we will need to branch the v1.4.0 release branch from the develop branch and when it is ready to release, merge that into master without inducing bad merge conflicts or creating Back to the Future Part II git history that would doom every future git bisect.

And there maybe other problems that I haven't considered yet. So, thoughts?

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] repositories in flux
parts:
On Friday, May 17, 2013 8:05:06 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Can't we just now

  * leave "master" branch as is

  * create a "develop" branch from "master" as it stands

I think that is a strong possibility also, but it would leave us in a state that is outside the gitflow paradigm. That is why Daniel was thinking about rewinding master to v1.3.0 and at some point in the next week or two merging a release branch (that was branched off develop) into (the "new" yet at v1.3.0) master. I don't know if that would go well or not.

Then in the future

  * push all "feature/" branches to "develop"

  * push all "hotfix/" branches to "master" and "develop"

  * push all "release/" branches to "master" and "develop"
Yes, that is just basic gitflow philosophy.

Is the issue that if you create the branch from "master"
you have to push it back into "master"?

That is possible in general, but I don't know about ultimately pushing it into a rewinded master without doing bad things to the history. These operations are vaguely akin to reverting a merge, which is always a last resort, and can be complicated in the best of circumstances

http://git-scm.com/blog/2010/03/02/undoing-merges.html

If so, can we
just merge all the branches we have back into "master"
before we start the above?

I think if a branch is finished, it should get merged into master before we start transitioning so that it is less likely to get lost. At some level, we'll probably have to take our chances with branches that are currently unfinished, but I hope they could be merged under the proposal I originally outlined.

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] repositories in flux
parts:
On Fri, May 17, 2013 at 9:09 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Friday, May 17, 2013 8:05:06 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> Can't we just now
>>
>> * leave "master" branch as is
>>
>>
>> * create a "develop" branch from "master" as it stands

I would support this transition plan. It seems the least likely to
disrupt existing branches and I don't really see a down side. That
our history doesn't follow gitflow is fine as, well, we *weren't*
using that paradigm before now.

As an alternative, we could continue using master as the "develop"
branch until we're ready for a 1.4/2.0 release. At which point master
becomes the real master, and we branch develop and continue working
off of that.

I really don't see a need to rush this and try to perform some kind of
git surgery, although I'd be interested to hear if anyone does see a
need.

Cheers,
Marcus
